blocks.text: It is proved that אנקה anaka of Levit. XI, 30. is a kind of stellio, so called from its harsh shrill cry.

Next, in Levit. XI, 30., follow five species of creeping things whose names are not easy to ex- [col. 1064] plain, since they are found nowhere else. They are אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. Of these, אנקה anaka is for the Greeks and for Jerome μυγάλη [mygalē] mygale, that is, the mus araneus [shrew]. They hold that it is called Μυγάλην [Mygalēn] because it is born ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς [ek myos kai galēs], from a mouse and a weasel. The scholiast on Nicander says: Ἀμύντας δή φησι τὴν μυγάλην ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς γίνεσθαι [Amyntas dē phēsi tēn mygalēn ek myos kai galēs ginesthai]. This is utterly absurd, since the weasel is much larger than the mouse and as hostile to it as the cat, as we observed above ^{a)}. That a weasel should mate with a mouse and a shrew be born of it is therefore wholly improbable. Aetius puts it better in the Tetrabiblos, book 4, sermon 1, chapter 14: The shrew is like the weasel in colour, but like the mouse in size; hence it also obtained the name mygale. Yet the shrew has the appearance of a mouse rather than its size, for it is altogether smaller than a mouse. The Romans seem to call it mus araneus [spider mouse] from its venom, which it shares with the spider. And in Hebrew it has been thought to be called אנקה anaka by reason of its voice, which is extremely shrill, so that it can be taken for a groan and a wail; for otherwise אנקה anaka means groaning or outcry to the Hebrews. If Onkelos understood the same, then in his Paraphrase, instead of ילא jala (the word by which אנקה anaka is rendered there), one must read פלא pala, or phala. For the Arabs call the shrew so. Avicenna, book 4, Fen 6, tract. 3, last chapter, in the title: فصل في عضة موغالي وهو الغلا [faṣl fī ʿaḍḍat mūghālī wa-huwa al-ghalā] Chapter on the bite of the mygale, which (for the Arabs) is alphala. In the Latin version one reads alcale, which would be الغلا [al-ghalā]. I should think that half-learned men changed one or the other into ילא jala. Under this name two very different animals occur in the Talmudic books, namely the leech and the hedgehog. But neither of them has a place here. For neither is called אנקה anaka in Hebrew; rather the hedgehog is called קפוד kippod, and the leech עלוקה aluka, or rather עלקה alka. Moreover, the subject here is those creeping things that creep upon the earth, and the leech is not of that number. So much for the first and most ancient interpretation of the word אנקה anaka.
